thread.title: Earnings Season Could Be the Savior This Anxious Stock Market Needs

author: Home
title: Earnings Season Could Be the Savior This Anxious Stock Market Needs
text:
Investors across the board struck a worrisome tone Wednesday, April 4, as the looming threat of a trade war sent U.S. stocks lower. But even in this time of uncharacteristically high volatility, earnings season could soon give Wall Street the bullish incentive it needs.
"The markets are strange now, but they've been strange forever," said Howard Silverblatt, senior index analyst for S&P Dow Jones Indices. But he noted that fundamentals are very strong -- cash hit a record in the fourth quarter and should continue to grow as repatriated funds following the passage of tax reform trickle in.
The big boon to the stock market isn't cash alone, though. It's earnings, Silverblatt said at an S&P Global panel in New York.
Earnings hit a record in the last quarter, and the trend looks to be sticking around. "This quarter, no matter who you use, we've got record numbers," Silverblatt said.
"For the first time since 2011, quarterly EPS has been revised up in the months leading into earnings season," Bank of America Merrill Lynch analysts wrote in a note Wednesday. Typically, analysts slash their outlooks by 3% to 4% in the weeks leading up to earnings season.
On average, analysts expect first-quarter earnings of $36.17, up 17% from last year. That outlook is also a pickup from up 15% growth in the fourth quarter of 2017, which was the best growth in six years, BofA wrote.
In an uncertain market, earnings strength could be just what the doctor ordered.
"Give them the worst scenario? You can trade around it," Silverblatt said. "The hope is that earnings season pulls you through."
Reporting for first-quarter financials begins on Friday, April 13 -- a spooky day for some superstitious traders. "Friday the 13th is actually a good day. The market goes up 56.2% of the time," Silverblatt said, adding that on any given other day the same likelihood of a gain is only 52%.
The first two big corporations to report will be JPMorgan Chase & Co. ( JPM ) and Wells Fargo & Co. ( WFC ) . They kick off a string of big bank earnings reports expected in mid-April.
"We'll see if JPMorgan and Wells Fargo agree," Silverblatt said. "But basically the markets are looking short-term, hoping to hold on."
And hold on they will. Silverblatt said he expects the S&P 500 should reach $1 trillion this year in dividends and buybacks. He suggested there's a race among Wall Street watchers and exchange floor traders -- what will hit $1 trillion first, the market cap of Apple Inc. ( AAPL ) or the S&P 500's total returns?
"I'll bet on the S&P definitely doing it because we're close to it with all this money coming in. Apple needs about another 17% from where they are now," Silverblatt said.
